CHAPTER III · THE CHURCH IN ACTS
The lame man at the temple gate
Now Peter and John went up together into the temple at the hour of prayer, being the ninth hour.
With Peter he goes up to the temple at the hour of prayer, where a lame man is healed (Acts 3:1–11).
And they, when they had testified and preached the word of the Lord, returned to Jerusalem, and preached the gospel in many villages of the Samaritans.
The apostles send Peter and John to Samaria; they pray for the believers, then preach “in many villages of the Samaritans” on the way back (Acts 8:14–25).

I John, who also am your brother, and companion in tribulation, and in the kingdom and patience of Jesus Christ, was in the isle that is called Patmos, for the word of God, and for the testimony of Jesus Christ.

The writer of Revelation calls himself John and says he “was in the isle that is called Patmos, for the word of God, and for the testimony of Jesus Christ” (Rev 1:9). Whether he is this John is disputed.
Tradition, by who said it and when · 11 sources
What Scripture says of his end
Jesus told James and John, “Ye shall indeed drink of the cup that I drink of” (Mark 10:39).
Of the beloved disciple a saying went round “that that disciple should not die: yet Jesus said not unto him, He shall not die” (John 21:23).
Revelation’s John was on Patmos “for the word of God, and for the testimony of Jesus Christ” (Rev 1:9).
Scripture does not record his death. Acts last shows him in Samaria (Acts 8:14–25) and then names him only as James’s brother (Acts 12:2).

Irenaeus has him at Ephesus “until the times of Trajan”; Polycrates says he “sleeps at Ephesus”; Jerome says he died “worn out by old age”.
Papias’s second book, as reported by Philip of Side (5th century) and George Hamartolus (9th century)

George Hamartolus says Papias wrote that John “was killed by the Jews, and thereby evidently fulfilled, together with his brother, Christ’s prophecy concerning them”. Lightfoot and Harmer (1891) print the first report with a question mark on its attribution to Philip of Side.
